name: Caregiving: Caring for a Loved One
objectives: Given a normal day with your loved one, list what they can do on their own and where they need help, in three groups: daily care, health care, and money and paperwork, after asking what matters most to them

Using a binder or a private file on your phone or computer, start a care notebook with contacts, conditions, allergies, insurance and where legal papers are kept, with no full private numbers typed into AI tools or emails

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Understanding your loved one's needs
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List what your loved one can do on their own and where they need help.
This lesson builds toward: Given a normal day with your loved one, you will list what they can do on their own and where they need help, in three groups: daily care, health care, and money and paperwork, after asking what matters most to them.
Caregivers help with many things. MedlinePlus lists washing, meals and medicines; housework, cooking and errands; rides to appointments; company and emotional support; coordinating medical care; and help with health and money decisions.
Start by looking at a normal day. What can your loved one do on their own? What do they find hard: bathing, dressing, cooking, remembering medicines, managing bills, getting to the doctor? Ask them, and listen. People want to keep as much independence and say over their own life as they can.
Write needs down in three groups: daily care, health care, and money and paperwork. This list shows you where help is needed most and what to ask others to do. Needs change over time, so look at it again every few months or after a hospital stay.
Step by step:
- Walk through a normal day with your loved one.
- List what they can do on their own.
- List where they need help: daily care, health care, money and paperwork.
- Ask what matters most to them.
- Review the list every few months or after a hospital stay.
Words to know:
- Caregiver: a person who helps someone who needs support because of age, illness or disability; often family or a friend.
- Independence: being able to do things and make choices for yourself.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Caregivers
Try it now: Write a needs list for your loved one (or someone you might care for one day) in three columns: daily care, health care, money and paperwork. Circle the two biggest needs.
You can now list your loved one's needs in daily care, health care and paperwork while respecting their independence.

check.q: Which three groups does the course use to sort a loved one's needs?
options: Daily care, health care, and money and paperwork
check.why: Sorting needs into daily care, health care, and money and paperwork shows where help is needed most.

check.q: Your father can still cook simple meals but forgets his pills. How do you plan help?
options: Take over all his cooking too
Do nothing until there is a problem
Help with medicines and let him keep cooking, as he wants
check.why: People want to keep as much independence as they can, so focus help where it is needed.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Building a care notebook
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Start a care notebook that keeps key information in one place.
This lesson builds toward: Using a binder or a private file on your phone or computer, you will start a care notebook with contacts, conditions, allergies, insurance and where legal papers are kept, with no full private numbers typed into AI tools or emails.
The CDC notes that a care plan can help caregivers keep important information in one place. Call it a care notebook: a binder, a folder or a document on your phone or computer that you, family helpers and a substitute caregiver can use.
What goes in it: contacts (doctors, pharmacy, family, neighbors, emergency contacts); a medicine list; health conditions and allergies; insurance information (Medicare, Medicaid, VA or private plan); an appointment calendar; and notes from each visit. Add a copy of any legal papers they have, such as a power of attorney or advance directive, and where the originals are kept.
Keep it safe and private. If you keep it on a computer or phone, use a password. Don't type full Medicare, Social Security or bank numbers into AI tools or emails. A grandchild who is good with technology can help set up a shared calendar or a simple document, with your loved one's permission.
Step by step:
- Choose paper (binder) or digital (phone or computer document).
- Add contacts, conditions, allergies and insurance.
- Add the medicine list and the appointment calendar.
- Note where legal papers are kept.
- Show one backup person where it is.
Words to know:
- Care plan: a written record of a person's needs, care and important information.
- Power of attorney: a legal paper that lets someone act for another person, for example with money or health decisions.
- Advance directive: a legal paper that says what medical care a person wants if they can't speak for themselves.
Official sources:
- CDC: Caregiving
Try it now: Start your care notebook today: on paper or on your phone, write the contacts page (doctor, pharmacy, two family members, emergency contact) and the allergies and conditions page.
You can now set up a care notebook that keeps contacts, health information and appointments in one place.

options: One place for key care information that you and helpers can use
check.why: A care notebook keeps contacts, medicines, insurance and appointments in one place.

check.q: You keep the care notebook on your phone. What do you do to keep it private?
options: Use a password and keep full Medicare and bank numbers out of AI tools and emails
Post it to social media for family
Email it to everyone you know
Paste it all into an AI assistant
check.why: Keep it safe with a password and do not type full private numbers into AI tools or emails.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Managing medicines and appointments
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Keep a medicine list and prepare questions for your loved one's next appointment.
This lesson builds toward: Given your loved one's medicines and next appointment, you will keep a complete medicine list and write questions for the doctor or pharmacist, never stopping, starting or changing a medicine without asking them.
Medicine mix-ups are common when someone takes several medicines. MedlinePlus advises keeping a list of every medicine with its dose and when it's taken, including over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, supplements and herbs, plus allergies, and bringing it to every visit. Read the label before every dose. A weekly pill organizer can help. Never stop, start or change a medicine without asking the doctor or pharmacist.
The pharmacist is a free expert. Ask: Why is this needed? What side effects should I watch for? Is it safe with the other medicines? Any foods or alcohol to avoid? Using one pharmacy for everything helps them catch problems.
For appointments, bring the care notebook, write questions ahead, take notes, and repeat the plan back to check you understood. Doctors' offices usually need your loved one's permission before sharing their health information with you; ask the office what form they use. For Medicare questions, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) and ask how your loved one can let you speak for them, or get free one-on-one help from your state's SHIP (shiphelp.org).
Step by step:
- Update the medicine list: name, dose, time, what it is for.
- Use one pharmacy and ask the pharmacist your questions.
- Use a pill organizer if it helps; read labels every time.
- Before a visit, write questions; during it, take notes and repeat the plan back.
- Ask the office what permission form lets you get information.
Words to know:
- Pill organizer: a box with spaces for each day (and time) to sort pills ahead.
- SHIP: State Health Insurance Assistance Program: free, local help with Medicare questions.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Medication Errors
- Medicare.gov: Talk to Someone
- SHIP: State Health Insurance Assistance Programs
Try it now: Add the medicine list to your care notebook: name, dose, time, what it is for. Then write three questions for your loved one's next appointment or for the pharmacist.
You can now keep an accurate medicine list, work with the pharmacist and prepare for appointments as a caregiver.

check.q: What belongs on a medicine list?
options: Only the medicines taken in the morning
Every medicine, vitamin, supplement and herb, with dose and time, plus allergies
check.why: A complete list helps the doctor and pharmacist catch problems.

check.q: The doctor explains a new plan quickly. How do you make sure you understood?
options: Repeat the plan back in your own words and take notes
check.why: Repeating the plan back checks that you understood it correctly.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Getting help and caring for yourself

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Finding help in your community
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find local caregiver services using the Eldercare Locator.
This lesson builds toward: When you need local help, you will contact the Eldercare Locator or another service to find caregiver support near you, writing what you learn in the care notebook.
You don't have to find everything yourself. The Eldercare Locator, a public service of the Administration for Community Living (ACL), connects older adults and caregivers to local services. Call or text 1-800-677-1116, chat online, or search by location at eldercare.acl.gov. It can connect you to your local Area Agency on Aging.
Through the National Family Caregiver Support Program, states and local agencies offer: information about services, help getting those services, counseling, support groups and caregiver training, respite care (a break for you), and some extra services. It covers adult family caregivers of people 60 and older, of people of any age with Alzheimer's disease or related conditions, and some older relatives raising children or caring for adults with disabilities. Ask what is available near you.
Caring for a veteran? The VA Caregiver Support Program helps caregivers of veterans enrolled in VA health care. Call the Caregiver Support Line at 1-855-260-3274, Monday to Friday, 8 am to 8 pm Eastern. For Medicare questions, your state's SHIP gives free local help.
Step by step:
- Call or text the Eldercare Locator: 1-800-677-1116, or search eldercare.acl.gov.
- Ask for your local Area Agency on Aging.
- Ask about caregiver training, support groups, respite care and meals.
- Caring for a veteran: call 1-855-260-3274.
- Write what you learn in your care notebook.
Words to know:
- Area Agency on Aging: a local office that helps older adults and caregivers find services.
- Respite care: short-term care for your loved one so you can take a break.
- ACL: Administration for Community Living, part of the US Department of Health and Human Services.
Official sources:
- Eldercare Locator (ACL)
- ACL: National Family Caregiver Support Program
- VA Caregiver Support Program
Try it now: Go to eldercare.acl.gov (or call or text 1-800-677-1116) and find your local Area Agency on Aging. Write its name, phone number and one service you want to ask about in your care notebook.
You can now find local caregiver help through the Eldercare Locator and your Area Agency on Aging, and know where veteran caregivers can call.

options: Short-term care so the caregiver can take a break
check.why: Respite care gives the caregiver a break, and local agencies may offer it.

check.q: You need meals and a support group near you but do not know where to start. What do you do?
options: Ask the doctor to find everything
Call or text the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116
check.why: The Eldercare Locator connects you to local services, including your Area Agency on Aging.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Sharing the load with family and friends
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask family and friends for specific help and set up a shared schedule.
This lesson builds toward: Given your list of needs, you will ask family and friends for specific tasks with a time and put them on a shared calendar, with at least two tasks taken on by others.
Many caregivers do everything alone because they don't want to bother anyone. People often want to help but don't know how. "Let me know if you need anything" rarely turns into help; a specific request does.
The CDC suggests naming a specific task or block of time you want help with and using a shared online calendar for regular help. MedlinePlus suggests letting helpers choose tasks they are comfortable with. Examples: "Can you drive Mom to her Thursday appointment?" "Can you call Dad every Sunday evening?" "Can you pick up groceries on Saturdays?" Family who live far away can handle bills, phone calls to insurance, research or video calls.
A short family meeting, in person or by video, helps everyone see the needs list and pick tasks. Include your loved one if they are able. If you work, ask your employer's human resources office about leave: under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act, eligible employees can take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave a year to care for certain family members.
Step by step:
- Take your needs list from Lesson 1.
- Turn needs into specific tasks with a time.
- Hold a short family meeting (in person or video).
- Let each helper choose tasks; put them on a shared calendar.
- Working? Ask HR about family leave.
Words to know:
- Shared calendar: an online calendar several people can see and add to.
- FMLA: the federal Family and Medical Leave Act, which lets eligible workers take unpaid leave to care for family.
Official sources:
- CDC: Caring for Yourself When Caring for Another
- MedlinePlus: Caregiver Health
Try it now: Write two specific requests (task, day and time) and send them to two people, or write who you would ask. Example: "Could you take Dad to his eye appointment on the 14th at 10 am?"
You can now turn needs into specific requests and share caregiving tasks with family and friends.

check.q: Why use a shared calendar for family help?
options: Everyone can see and sign up for tasks
check.why: A shared calendar lets helpers see needs and pick tasks.

check.q: Your brother says, "Let me know if you need anything." What is the best reply?
options: "Could you take Mom grocery shopping every Saturday morning?"
check.why: A specific task with a time is much more likely to turn into real help.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Caring for yourself as a caregiver
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot signs of caregiver stress and plan regular breaks.
This lesson builds toward: As a caregiver, you will check yourself for signs of caregiver stress and plan a regular break, with one weekly break and someone to cover for you.
The CDC puts it simply: to be an effective caregiver, you must take care of yourself. MedlinePlus lists signs of caregiver stress: feeling overwhelmed or alone, sleeping too much or too little, big weight changes, constant tiredness, losing interest in things you enjoyed, irritability or anger, frequent worry or sadness, frequent headaches or body aches, and smoking or drinking more.
What helps: regular breaks (even a few hours of respite a week can help), asking others for help, a caregiver support group (in person or online), staying in touch with friends, and looking after your own health with activity, healthy meals, sleep and your own checkups. Tell your own doctor you are a caregiver; they may know of support groups.
If you feel hopeless or overwhelmed and it doesn't get better, talk to your doctor or a counselor. In a crisis in the US, call or text 988; veterans and their families can press 1. Now you are ready to finish your care notebook and help plan.
Step by step:
- Check yourself against the signs of caregiver stress.
- Plan one regular break each week, and who covers for you.
- Find a caregiver support group (ask your Area Agency on Aging).
- Keep your own doctor visits and tell your doctor you are a caregiver.
- Crisis: call or text 988.
Words to know:
- Caregiver stress: the physical and emotional strain of caring for someone.
- Support group: a group of people in a similar situation who meet to share experiences and tips.
Official sources:
- MedlinePlus: Caregiver Health
- CDC: Caring for Yourself When Caring for Another
- 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
Try it now: Final task: finish your starter care notebook (contacts, medicine list, appointments and questions) and add a one-page help plan: one local resource you contacted or will contact, two specific tasks for family or friends, and your self-care plan with one weekly break.
You can now spot caregiver stress, plan regular breaks and keep caring for your loved one without losing your own health.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Care notebook Key contacts are missing, or full private numbers are written where others can see them. Key contacts, upcoming appointments and where legal papers are kept, all in one place. A backup person knows where the notebook is and how to use it. Medicines and next visit The medicine list is incomplete, or there are no questions for the next visit. A complete medicine list with dose and time, and written questions for the next appointment. Includes vitamins, supplements and allergies, and questions for the pharmacist. Local help No local resource named. One local resource contacted or planned, such as the Eldercare Locator. Wrote in the notebook what services are available and next steps. Shared tasks Tasks are vague, such as "help out", or fewer than two. Two specific tasks with a time, to ask family or friends to take on. Helpers have agreed and the tasks are on a shared calendar. Self-care plan No break planned. A self-care plan with one weekly break and someone to cover. Also names a support group or tells their own doctor they are a caregiver. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a sign of caregiver stress?
options: Feeling overwhelmed, alone or constantly tired
check.why: Feeling overwhelmed or alone and constant tiredness are signs of caregiver stress.

check.q: You have not had a break in months. What is a good first step?
options: Keep going until you get sick
Stop caring for your loved one
Plan one regular weekly break and ask someone to cover for you
check.why: Even a few hours of respite a week can help, with someone covering for you.
